Reading the averages: waiting, onboard and total journey averages include completed passengers in each system; those groups can differ. Check the waiting and riding counts too. The saving above compares the same completed passengers.

What is a ride? Here it is one vehicle leg between two stops, not a passenger booking or a whole multi-stop tour. Average load includes empty repositioning and scheduled empty trips. Seat utilization is weighted by actual driving time.

Synthetic demand, distances and timetables. Explore the assumptions before using the results.

Inside the simulation

This simulation covers Dorflinie Bus only. Dorflinie Car is a separate service and is not modeled here. Dorflinie Bus explores pooled, on-demand rural bus transport: book a destination and an arrival deadline, then share a shuttle with compatible journeys.

A fair passenger comparison

Both systems receive the exact same seeded Poisson arrival stream. 60% of origins are Hbf; village departures mainly go to Hbf, with some trips between villages. Train-wave mode concentrates demand into five minutes every half hour. No future passenger requests are revealed to the shuttle planner.

Scheduled buses

Each active city has a radial scheduled service to Hbf. Outbound departures are staggered by the selected headway divided by the city count. Buses return after the outbound drive and one minute at the village. Each departure has 30 seats; overflow waits for the next departure. Village-to-village passengers transfer at Hbf with a minimum two-minute connection. The timetable may require overlapping vehicles at shorter headways.

Deadline-aware shuttle insertion

Every minute, unassigned requests are ordered by deadline and waiting age. For each vehicle, the planner tries pickup and dropoff insertions while keeping existing stop order, respecting seat capacity on every leg and preserving a moving vehicle’s next stop. It chooses the smallest incremental route cost: route duration + 0.25 × total journey minutes + 20 × late minutes. Every stop takes one minute. Routes are limited to 20 stops to keep planning responsive. This is an insertion heuristic; it does not guarantee optimal routes or on-time arrival. Pending requests are retried each minute.

What the figures mean

All road speeds are 35 km/h, with drive times rounded up to full minutes. The original A/B/C roads stay unchanged. Added cities have deterministic synthetic distances, with Hbf distances shown on the map. Inter-city distances are synthetic direct roads. Adding cities keeps existing road distances and the total arrival rate unchanged; use the demand control to model population growth. The map rearranges stops for legibility and is not real geography.

Average wait, journey time and on-time rate include only completed journeys in that scenario. The saving at the top uses only the same passengers completed in both by the current time. Queued and onboard riders stay visible and are not counted as completed. An ETA comes from the current route plan; it can change with new requests. Unassigned riders show “Unassigned” rather than an invented ETA. Timetable wait includes transfer wait; shuttle wait is time before pickup.

Limits & next steps

This is a concept model, not a transport service or a validated operational forecast. Fleet resources differ: three scheduled lines versus the chosen number of shuttles. There is no equal-cost or emissions claim. Walking, traffic, wheelchair boarding, driver breaks, cancellations and operating costs are excluded. Real testing needs local timetable, road and demand data. FlixBus-style booking and parcel-style pooling are inspirations; there is no affiliation with FlixBus or Amazon.

Test your own connection

Add one passenger to both scenarios. Give them a destination and a time they need to arrive.

The simulation pauses at your arrival so you can follow the trip. Very tight deadlines may be missed.
